paras: The lynching of J. J. Dickison Jr. was the killing of a prisoner in the jail at Leesburg, Sumter County, Florida, by a party of armed and disguised men at about 2 a.m. on Friday, July 15, 1881. Dickison, the son of a former Adjutant General of Florida, had been jailed the evening before, accused of shooting a Leesburg man named Beach with a shotgun. A coroner's jury attributed his death to unknown parties, and Florida editors widely condemned the killing, while the Leesburg paper argued that his record explained it.

Dickison, described in a Jacksonville dispatch as the son of "General Dickinson, late Adjutant-General of Florida," had come to Leesburg more than a year earlier; the Leesburg Advance said he had left Quincy secretly "for shooting a negro." By its account, on June 28 he quarreled with Lewis Beach at S. W. Wallace's barroom and fired at him; Beach fired back and hit him in the arm, and Dickison was released under a $500 peace bond.

A different version of an earlier fight came from the Ocala Banner, reprinted in the Weekly Floridian on July 12, which said Dickinson had been shot "three or four times" by "a Mr. Blitch" and was reported to have been the aggressor.

On the night of Monday, July 11, according to the Advance, Dickison fired a concealed shotgun at Beach behind Baer's store, filling his shoulder with buckshot. The Jacksonville wire placed the shooting on "last Tuesday" and said Beach was "severely but not dangerously wounded." A sheriff's posse tracked him across the Ocklawaha River and found him asleep in a house at daylight on Thursday, July 14; he surrendered and was jailed in Leesburg that evening under guard.

At about two o'clock the next morning a masked party of twenty-five to thirty men overpowered the guards, forced them to open the door, and shot him with double-barreled guns. The wire version said the men shot him twice in his cell and "then took him outside and riddled him with bullets"; the Advance did not mention his being taken outside.

A coroner's inquest found that he died "by shots from guns in the hands of unknown parties," and he was buried in Lone Oak Cemetery. No report of arrests, an indictment or a trial of any of the men was found in the coverage. Other Florida papers called for action: the Manatee News said the lynching "should at once be handled without gloves by our executives of the law," and the Apopka Citizen urged a public meeting in every town in the state to condemn "the Leesburg tragedy."

A Jacksonville dispatch of July 16 carried the story the next day to Richmond, Chicago and Memphis and within days as far as Sacramento. Headlines over the same text varied widely: "A Florida Lynching" in Richmond, "Lynched in Florida" in Savannah, "A revenge" in Chicago, "Summary Justice" in Rock Island, "Served Him Right" in Memphis and "A Would-be Assassin Killed in Florida" in Sacramento.

The Savannah Morning News added that the young man, once his father's clerk there, "will doubtless be remembered by many of our citizens." The Leesburg Advance, reprinted in Savannah under the headline "The Leesburg Tragedy," said it did "not approve of lynch law" but wrote that leading citizens "feel much relieved at the death of Mr. Dickison." The Weekly Floridian in Tallahassee, which said he was lynched "under the erroneous impression that Beach was fatally wounded," called it the first case in the state with "so little shadow of excuse," and the Fernandina Mirror welcomed the "strong and united voice of the press of Florida" against it.
None of the reports gives the race of Dickison, Beach or the men who killed him, and no paper framed the killing in racial terms.

The accounts differ on the earlier fight: the Advance said Beach wounded Dickison in the arm on June 28, while the Ocala Banner named the other man as Blitch and said Dickison was hit three or four times. They also differ on the date Beach was shot (July 11 in the Advance, "last Tuesday" in the wire) and on his wound, which a later digest called "dangerous."

bases: A jailed prisoner accused of shooting a man was killed in or at the Leesburg jail by 25-30 armed, disguised men who overpowered his guards (A2, A17).

An armed, masked party of 25-30 men overpowered the jail guards and shot Dickison dead; the coroner's jury named 'unknown parties' and the press called it lynching (A2, A17, A12). The pretext was his alleged shooting of Beach and his record as a 'desperado', which the local paper offered as the reason for 'lynch law' (A17).

The Jacksonville wire (A2, A7) and the independent local Leesburg Advance account (A17) agree on the jailing and the killing by a disguised party of about 25 men; Florida editorials confirm it (A12, A27).

accounts.label: Jacksonville wire report
accounts.gist: Dickinson renewed an old difficulty by shooting saloon-keeper Beach 'last Tuesday'; captured and jailed, he was shot twice in prison by 25 armed and disguised men, then taken outside and riddled with bullets.

accounts.label: Leesburg Advance (local paper)
accounts.gist: Gives Dickison's record as a 'desperado', the June 28 fight and the July 11 shotgun ambush of Beach; a sheriff's posse captured him; 25-30 masked men overpowered the guards and shot him; the inquest found unknown parties responsible.

accounts.label: Ocala Banner (earlier affray)
accounts.gist: Reported a Leesburg affray in which Dickinson was shot three or four times by a Mr. Blitch, with Dickinson said to be the aggressor.

accounts.label: Tallahassee editorial
accounts.gist: Says Dickison was lynched under the mistaken belief that Beach was fatally wounded and that the case had less excuse than any other in the state.

framing.detail: National papers ran the Jacksonville wire under headlines from 'A Florida Lynching' and 'Lynched in Florida' to 'A revenge', 'Summary Justice', 'Served Him Right' and 'A Would-be Assassin Killed'.
The Leesburg Advance said it did 'not approve of lynch law' but published Dickison's record at citizens' request to show why 'such severe measures were resorted to'.
The Weekly Floridian called it 'unfortunate and horrible' with 'so little shadow of excuse'; the Fernandina Mirror, Manatee News and Apopka Citizen also denounced it.
The Savannah Morning News noted the victim's local ties and his father's standing without comment on the lynching.
